correctness.rationale: For every real 2x2 SPD A,K, Cayley–Hamilton reduces the nuclear residual to det(A)*(g^Tg)/(g^TAg). The uniform-circle matrix ratio identity E[uu^T/(u^TCu)]=(C+sqrt(det C)I)^(-1) is proved by a complete integral and two linear identities. An exact 2x2 inverse calculation gives the trace/determinant formula; derivative-sign analysis shows no finite strict interior anisotropy minimum and provides the arctan fourth-root switch. High-r joint asymptotics are uniform in paths with r→∞ and θ→0. Standalone tests passed 712 assertions, supporting rather than replacing the analytic proof.

originality.rationale: Direct inspection of arXiv:2404.00960 Sections 2.1–2.2, arXiv:2209.11023 Sections 2–3, and arXiv:1706.05736 Sections 2–4 identified general correlated Gaussian Nyström bounds, isotropic Gaussian constructions and matrix-function extensions but not the exact rank-one planar covariance dependence or optimal uncertainty-angle phase threshold. Published and prior isotropic two-coordinate Gaussian range-projection results can imply a special case, which is acknowledged and not claimed. Search cannot rule out an unindexed equivalent generic Gaussian-ratio formula; that is a residual precedence risk.
residual_risks: A generic theorem on expectations of ratios of correlated Gaussian quadratic forms may already yield the formula indirectly, although no inspected published Nyström theorem establishes the sharp angular-information minimax conclusion.
The scope is two-dimensional and one-column; no unique literature precedence is asserted.
Further specialist manual comparison could reveal an equivalent covariance-optimization result under different terminology.

value.rationale: The smallest nontrivial covariance-aware Nyström experiment has a complete sharp solution: one exact risk formula, a robust no-interior-optimum theorem, a condition-number-dependent critical angular information threshold, and a two-scale precision law. This meaningfully quantifies when using an estimated eigendirection improves or harms expected nuclear error, a distinction suggested but not quantified sharply by general covariance-quality bounds. The result is a benchmark, not a claim of practical superiority against complete eigensolvers or multidimensional methods.
